raw_tweets.text: Amazing progress so far! Qwen 3.8 27B is now 170% faster on Apple Sillicon. https://t.co/fTuYP6RTfv

profile_bio.description: Fascinated by greatness and exploring the open frontier | Eigen Labs (Darkbloom, Yukon...)

quoted_tweet.text:
Apple Silicon is built for MoE models -- huge unified memory, modest bandwidth. Dense models are the opposite: bandwidth-bound, and everyone "knows" Macs are slow at them.  

Today we're changing that. https://t.co/liyzSFqLAa is now improving Qwen3.8 27B from @QwenDevs. Under 16 hours in: +153% over baseline. 2.5x faster than out of the box MTP decode.  

I think that's barely the start. When a belief is that widely held (Mac is slow at dense models), few has gone looking. The low-hanging fruit is still there.  

We've improved based on feedback from the last challenge.

- MTP on day 1. Speculative decoding is the whole game for dense models, and the draft head weights are yours to edit. 
- 8 hidden length, not 1. Laguna's score overfit a single 512-token fixture. Now every run is the median across eight weights. 
- New leaderboard. Ranks total improvement contributed, not who happens to hold the record right now. The old view lives on as the lineage board (better name welcome). 
- Automated review. Every submission gets screened for benchmark gaming before it scores.  

Next up: enabling multiplatform starting with CUDA.

raw_tweets.text:
DeepSeek did it again.

They quietly published a paper that fixes THE fundamental bug in every transformer ever trained.

Every major AI model you use today is relies on something called the residual connection.

Since ResNets in 2016, neural networks have used simple, additive shortcuts to pass information from one layer to the next. 

It’s what allowed deep learning to go from a few layers to hundreds without exploding or vanishing gradients.

It became the invisible law of AI architecture.

When you try to scale up standard residual streams or use "Hyper-Connections" to expand network capacity, things break down catastrophically. 

Without strict constraints, information starts compounding.

Signals amplify. Matrix values spiral out of control. Amplification factors hit 3,000x in practice.

Training crashes. Loss curves explode.

Every major lab knew the architecture was hitting a wall.

Then DeepSeek quietly published a paper fixing it at the mathematical root.

They call it Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC).

Instead of letting information streams multiply blindly, DeepSeek used a 1946 mathematical concept, the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm, to project the mixing matrices onto a constrained manifold.

Every single stream is forced to balance out.

Nothing explodes. Nothing vanishes.

The math guarantees total preservation.

The instability dropped from a 3,000x explosion down to a controlled 1.6x.

They engineered the hardware execution down to the metal, fusing kernels and slashing memory traffic so it runs at massive scale without dragging down inference speeds.
